content: The iTE Doctors program utilizes FibroScan machines and full laboratory capabilities to support hepatitis C (HCV) care. Patient screening is conducted through rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) via active case finding in local villages and passive case finding in rural health centers. Pre-treatment assessments are performed during HCV viral load (VL) appointments. A simplified hepatitis C training program is provided for nurses, general practitioners (GPs), and laboratory technicians. The training curriculum includes a two-day session for GPs and nurses, while laboratory technicians, already familiar with Xpert technology from tuberculosis programs, undergo a one-day session. For uncomplicated cases, patients receive a daily oral dose of Sofosbuvir (SOF) and Daclatasvir (DCV) 400/60 mg for 12 weeks, with prescriptions provided monthly. Complicated cases are referred to secondary-level referral hospitals for further assessment by GPs. Nurses monitor treatment adherence during the first and second months of therapy. Regular supervision is conducted for health center nurses monthly initially, transitioning to quarterly reviews later. Uncomplicated cases are managed at health centers, where nurses initiate direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy, perform HCV RDTs, point-of-care VL sampling, HIV testing, pregnancy testing, and hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) testing. Patients receive monthly medication refills, with an optional sustained virologic response (SVR12) VL test. By the third visit, patients without complications receive a two-month medication refill. Complicated cases, such as those presenting with jaundice, encephalopathy, gastrointestinal bleeding, ascites, or edema, are managed at referral hospitals. Doctors initiate DAA therapy and oversee follow-up care. Nurses triage patients, directing uncomplicated cases to health centers and complicated cases to referral hospitals. In a nurse-led pilot program, 547 patients were enrolled. Of these, 204 were referred to GPs at referral hospitals, while 329 uncomplicated cases completed treatment under nurse supervision. Fourteen patients did not return for post-treatment testing, including two deaths unrelated to HCV treatment and 12 lost to follow-up. Among the 310 patients who completed treatment, 98% achieved SVR12, while 2% experienced treatment failure. The pilot project demonstrated the feasibility of decentralized and simplified HCV care pathways integrated into primary healthcare services. This approach reduces costs and allows task-shifting for uncomplicated cases without compromising treatment safety or efficacy. Simplified and decentralized HCV services are essential for scaling up hepatitis C care and treatment, regardless of a country’s income classification. Globally, approximately 7% of the population is hepatitis C antibody-positive, with over 1 million people living with hepatitis C. Transmission occurs through formal and informal healthcare settings and injecting drug use. Among people who inject drugs, 56% are hepatitis C antibody-positive. National hepatitis control programs provide services at 13 hospital sites. The CT2 study in Yangon, Myanmar, demonstrated the effectiveness of a one-stop-shop model for community-based hepatitis C testing and treatment. Decentralized, task-shifted services in urban Myanmar were found to be feasible and scalable, with significant implications for expanding access to care.
